title: Fine-Tuning: Teach an AI Your Job
subtitle: Take a giant model and tailor it without rebuilding it
intro: A giant AI already knows the internet, but not your business. What if you could teach it your job in an afternoon on one GPU?
takeaway: Fine-tuning teaches a big model a new skill cheaply with small adapters, but bad data teaches bad habits.

sections.heading: Analogy: tailoring a suit, not weaving fabric
sections.body:
Imagine buying a suit off the rack and tailoring it to fit you. You don't remake the fabric — you add small darts and hems.

Fine-tuning is like that. You start with a pre-trained LLM and add tiny adjustments so it fits your task.

That sets up why we don't train from scratch next.

sections.heading: Why does this exist? Your own model without mega-cost
sections.body:
Training from scratch costs millions. Fine-tuning reuses what the model knows and teaches just the new part.

Two tricks make it cheap:
- Quantization with bitsandbytes: shrinks the model to fit on one GPU, like compressing a photo.
- LoRA / PEFT: Low-Rank Adaptation adds small trainable adapters instead of changing all weights.

You format examples with a template and train with SFTTrainer from Hugging Face, then run it locally with Ollama.

Cheap and private sounds perfect — until it goes wrong.

sections.heading: What can go wrong? Small data, big mistakes
sections.body:
If your dataset is messy, biased, or too small, the model memorizes mistakes and gets worse at everything else.

Quantization can also lower quality, and over-training makes it forget general knowledge.

Fix: use clean, balanced examples, test on held-out data, and keep adapters small.

steps.narration: Start with a giant pre-trained model that already knows language.
Shrink it with quantization so it fits on your GPU.
Attach tiny LoRA adapters — only these will learn.
Prepare clean examples in a consistent template.
Fine-tune just the adapters with SFTTrainer.
Run your tailored model privately with Ollama.

quiz.q: What does LoRA (PEFT) do when fine-tuning?
options: Adds small trainable adapters while freezing most weights
Deletes the base model to save space
quiz.why: LoRA freezes the big model and trains tiny low-rank adapters, making fine-tuning cheap and fast.

options: To make the model fit on a smaller GPU by using fewer bits per weight
To deploy with Ollama without training
To increase model size for accuracy
quiz.why: Quantization compresses weights (e.g., to 4-bit) so a large LLM fits in limited GPU memory.

quiz.q: What breaks first if you fine-tune on a tiny, messy dataset?
options: The model memorizes errors, gets biased, and forgets general skills
Ollama can no longer run locally
quiz.why: Bad data causes overfitting and forgetting — the model learns your noise instead of a useful skill.

extra: QLoRA combines 4-bit quantization + LoRA for single-GPU fine-tuning of 7B+ models.
